introduction: Today is World Mission Sunday. The Pharisees try to trap Jesus with a question about taxes, but he turns it into a question about belonging: the coin bears Caesar's image, and we bear God's. Isaiah reminds us that the Lord can work even through a pagan king, and Paul thanks God that the Gospel reached Thessalonica "not in word only, but also in power." As we gather around the altar, let us offer God what is already his: ourselves, and our part in the Church's mission to the whole world.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, we belong to God, who sends his Church to every nation. With confidence, let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church throughout the world: that, sent as Christ was sent, she may proclaim the Gospel with joy, in word and in deeds of love. Let us pray to the Lord.

For missionaries, priests, religious and lay people, especially those far from home and those studying to serve the Church: that the Holy Spirit may strengthen them in hardship and bless their work. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who hold public office: that they may serve the common good with honesty and never forget that their authority is given for the people. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who have not yet heard the Good News, and for those who have drifted from the faith: that they may meet Christ through the witness of believers. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our parish community: that we may give to God what is God's, generously supporting the missions by our prayer, our sacrifices and our gifts. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you have stamped your image on every human heart. Hear the prayers of your people, and make us faithful witnesses of your Son to the ends of the earth. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Whose image do you bear?
reflection.body:
The question put to Jesus was meant as a trap. If he said, "Pay the tax," he would anger the crowds who hated Roman rule; if he said, "Do not pay," he could be reported to the governor. Jesus asks for a coin and puts a question of his own: "Whose is this image and inscription?" Caesar's, they answer. Then give Caesar what is his, and give God what is God's.

The answer is not only clever. It sends us back to the first page of Scripture, where God makes man and woman in his own image. A coin carries the emperor's face; the human person carries God's. Caesar may claim a share of our money, but no ruler can claim the heart. That belongs to the One whose likeness it bears.

Isaiah offers a surprising picture of the same truth. Cyrus, a Persian king who did not know the Lord, is called God's "anointed" because through him the exiles will go home. God remains Lord of history even when rulers do not acknowledge him. We need not be anxious when the powers of this world seem to have the last word; they do not.

On World Mission Sunday this becomes a call. If every person bears God's image, then every person has a right to hear of the God who made them and redeemed them in Christ. Paul gives thanks for the Thessalonians, remembering their "work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope." Mission begins there: not in grand plans, but in faith that works, love that labors and hope that does not give up.

We may not all be sent to distant lands, though we pray today for those who are. But all of us are sent to someone: a neighbour, a colleague, a family member who no longer prays. This week, let us ask ourselves where we are holding back from God what already belongs to him, and give it back, gladly.
